questions.stem: A grocery chain forecasts weekly demand for 8,000 products with a statistical model whose accuracy has been tracked against actual sales for three years. Leadership has asked to "use Claude for forecasting". When you interview the demand planners, their real complaint is that they cannot tell why a forecast moved, so they distrust it and override it by hand. Which solution design BEST addresses the business problem?

options.text: Paste each product's sales history into a Claude prompt with several worked forecasting examples and have Claude produce the weekly forecast numbers directly
Deploy an autonomous agent with code execution that rebuilds and replaces the forecasting model every week using whatever technique it judges best that week
Keep the tracked statistical model for the numbers and have Claude turn its outputs and drivers into plain-language explanations that planners can question
Replace the statistical model with the most capable Claude model and instruct it to double-check its own arithmetic before returning each forecast number

questions.explanation: The stated request ("use Claude for forecasting") is not the actual problem. The problem is **trust and explainability**: planners override forecasts they cannot understand. Numeric time-series forecasting is already handled by a model with a measured track record. Claude adds value where language matters: explaining the drivers behind a change (promotions, seasonality, a price change) in plain words and answering planners' follow-up questions. This keeps the proven deterministic component and puts Claude on the language-shaped part of the problem.

whyWrong.A: It swaps a validated numeric model for an LLM doing arithmetic over long tables. Accuracy gets worse and harder to audit, and the explainability complaint is still not addressed.
whyWrong.B: This is over-engineered and risky. An agent that changes the production model every week removes the stable track record planners need, and it does nothing about explanations.
whyWrong.D: Neither a bigger model nor a self-check makes an LLM a better numeric forecaster than a validated statistical model, and the real problem (planners don't understand the forecasts) is still unsolved.

questions.mindset: Solve the business problem behind the request, and give Claude the language-shaped part rather than the part a proven deterministic system already does well.

questions.stem: A furniture retailer wants Claude to write product descriptions in its brand voice. Marketing has a 30-page style guide and 20 descriptions they consider perfect. They want something working within two weeks, and they expect the voice to keep changing as the brand evolves. Which approach is the BEST starting point?

options.text: Put condensed style rules and a few approved descriptions, wrapped in clear tags, into the system prompt, then test the drafts against a reviewer rubric
Collect several thousand more approved descriptions and train a custom model on them before launch, so the brand voice is built into the model's weights
Build an agent that browses competitors' product pages each day and adapts the tone of each description to whatever style currently appears to perform best
Let Claude write descriptions freely with no style guidance, and have marketing copy editors rewrite every description into the brand voice before it goes live

questions.explanation: Voice and style are exactly what **prompting** controls well: clear instructions, a few good examples (multishot prompting) and XML tags to separate the guide from the task. Prompting is fast to set up, cheap to change when the brand evolves, and can be checked against a rubric built from what reviewers care about. Heavier options only make sense if a measured gap remains after this.

whyWrong.B: Training a custom model is slow and needs a large dataset the team doesn't have. Each brand change would also mean retraining, which conflicts with both the two-week timeline and the expectation that the voice keeps evolving.
whyWrong.C: This copies other companies instead of following the retailer's own brand, and it adds a lot of complexity no one asked for.
whyWrong.D: It throws away the guidance Claude could use and pushes all the work back to humans, so it saves little effort.

questions.mindset: Start with the lightest lever that can meet the goal. For tone and style, that is a well-built prompt with examples, measured against a rubric.

questions.stem: A travel company handles customer support in nine languages. The current plan is to send every inbound message through a separate machine-translation service into English, have Claude answer in English, and translate the reply back. Stakeholders are worried about extra latency, added cost, and losing nuance in complaints. Which design is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Fine-tune a separate model for each of the nine languages so that every market has its own specialist model that handles its own customer traffic end to end
Keep the translation pipeline and add a second Claude call after each translation step to check the translation and correct any errors before passing it on
Ask customers to write in English whenever they can, and send messages in other languages to a separate queue staffed by bilingual human agents only
Let Claude read and answer in the customer's own language, set the reply language explicitly in the system prompt, and test each language with native-speaker evals

questions.explanation: Claude works well across many languages, so a translate-in, translate-out pipeline adds latency, cost and another place for meaning to get lost. Anthropic's guidance is to set the target language explicitly, preferably in the system prompt, and to test with the languages you will actually serve. Per-language evals with native speakers matter because performance varies by language.

whyWrong.A: Nine separate custom models multiply build and maintenance effort for a capability the base model already has.
whyWrong.B: This keeps every problem of the translation pipeline and adds one more model call per step, so cost and latency go up.
whyWrong.C: It shifts the burden onto customers and humans and does not use the multilingual support that would solve the problem.

questions.mindset: Before building scaffolding around a capability, check whether the model already has it, then verify it with evals.

questions.stem: A mid-sized manufacturer has a list of seven possible Claude use cases. The CIO wants the first pilot to show measurable value within one quarter and to build trust with a cautious risk committee before larger rollouts. Which TWO selection criteria BEST fit these goals? Choose TWO.

options.text: Choose the use case with the most executive visibility, one that touches every department at once, so the pilot attracts attention across the whole company
Choose a high-volume, repetitive task where today's baseline, such as time per item or error rate, is already measured and can be compared after launch
Choose the use case that needs the most sophisticated multi-agent architecture, to show the risk committee everything the platform can do
Choose the use case whose source data is scattered and hardest to reach, since that is where AI would unlock the most value that is currently hidden
Choose a task where mistakes are low-impact and reversible, or where a person reviews the output before it takes effect, so the risk stays contained

questions.explanation: A first pilot should **prove value and earn trust**. A measured baseline lets you show a before-and-after improvement within the quarter. Low-impact, reversible errors, or a human check before anything takes effect, keep the risk small, and that is what a cautious risk committee needs to see before approving bigger rollouts.

whyWrong.A: A company-wide use case has the most stakeholders, the largest blast radius and the slowest delivery, which is the opposite of a contained first pilot.
whyWrong.C: Complexity is not value. A sophisticated multi-agent design adds risk and delivery time, and it is harder to explain to a cautious committee.
whyWrong.D: When the data is hard to reach, most of the quarter goes into data plumbing before any value can be shown.

questions.mindset: The first pilot should be measurable, contained and reversible. Trust is earned in small steps.

questions.stem: An insurer's COO asks you to "make claim-file summaries better" with Claude. Adjusters currently spend about 12 minutes reading each file before deciding next steps. Before any design work starts, you need a success criterion that will guide the architecture and let the team tell objectively whether the solution works. Which criterion is BEST?

options.text: Summaries should be accurate, concise and professional in tone, as judged by the adjusters who will use them in their day-to-day work once the solution has launched
On 500 files already summarized by senior adjusters, 95% of AI summaries contain every required field, under 1% add a fact not in the file, and review time is under 5 minutes
The solution should use the most capable model available, with low temperature settings, so that the summaries it produces are as high in quality as possible
Adjusters should give the new summaries an average rating of at least 4.5 out of 5 in a satisfaction survey that is run once at the end of the first month

questions.explanation: Good success criteria are **specific, measurable, achievable and relevant**. Option B names a test set, a coverage threshold for required fields, a tight measurable limit on unsupported facts, and the business outcome (review time), all of which can be tested before and after launch. That gives the architecture something concrete to aim at and gives the team a clear pass or fail.

whyWrong.A: "Accurate, concise, professional" is the classic vague criterion. It cannot be measured consistently, so nobody can tell whether a design change helped.
whyWrong.C: This describes an implementation choice, not an outcome. It also locks in cost before anyone knows whether a smaller model would meet the goal.
whyWrong.D: A single satisfaction score at the end of the month is a lagging, subjective signal. It cannot catch fabricated facts and arrives too late to guide design.

questions.mindset: Turn a vague business wish into measurable success criteria before choosing any architecture.

questions.stem: An online retailer gets about 30,000 refund requests a month. Most fall under clear policy rules (time since purchase, item category, order value), but a minority need discretionary goodwill decisions. Once a refund is paid it is very hard to recover. Leadership wants as much automation as possible **while keeping financial exposure tightly controlled and auditable**. Which design BEST meets this?

options.text: Claude reads each request and gathers order facts via tools, a rules engine auto-approves in-policy refunds under a set amount, and exceptions go to staff with Claude’s summary
An autonomous agent receives the full refund policy in its system prompt and the ability to issue refunds, with instructions to be conservative and to refuse anything it is unsure about
Claude decides and issues every refund itself, records its reasoning for each decision, and the finance team reviews a monthly report of those logs to catch any problem patterns
Every request goes to a human agent, with Claude only drafting a summary of the request so the agent can read the case a bit faster before making the decision

questions.explanation: Match autonomy to **reversibility and risk**. Refunds are hard to undo, so the approve or deny decision for routine cases belongs in deterministic, auditable rules with a hard amount limit. Claude does the language work: understanding a free-text request and collecting the facts. Discretionary goodwill cases go to people, with Claude's summary and recommendation to speed them up. Most volume is automated, and exposure stays bounded and auditable.

whyWrong.B: Instructions in a prompt are not a control. "Be conservative" cannot guarantee a spending limit on an action that is hard to reverse, and it is weak evidence for an audit.
whyWrong.C: A monthly review finds problems only after money has been paid, and a record of reasoning does not stop bad refunds from going out.
whyWrong.D: This is safe but gives up most of the automation leadership asked for, even though most cases are rule-based and could be handled automatically.

questions.mindset: When an action is hard to reverse, put the decision in deterministic controls and use Claude to understand requests and gather facts.

questions.stem: A contact center wants live agent assist: while a call is in progress, a suggested answer should start appearing within about two seconds of the customer finishing a question, drawing on a 600-article knowledge base. The prototype runs the largest model at maximum reasoning effort, puts the entire knowledge base into every request, and waits for the complete response before showing anything, which takes about 15 seconds. Which redesign is MOST likely to meet the latency target without losing answer quality?

options.text: Send the suggestion requests through the Message Batches API so they run at lower cost, and show each suggestion to the agent as soon as the batch result becomes available
Keep the largest model at maximum reasoning effort and make prompt caching of the knowledge base the only change, because caching removes almost all of the delay
Pre-generate a summary of every knowledge-base article overnight, and during calls show the agent the summary whose title best matches the customer's question
Retrieve only the few most relevant articles, use a faster model tier that passes the quality eval, keep the output short, and stream it so the first words appear right away

questions.explanation: Latency comes from model size and effort, the number of input tokens, the number of output tokens, and whether the user has to wait for the whole response. Anthropic's latency guidance covers each one: choose a faster model that still meets quality on your eval, keep input and output lean (retrieving a few relevant articles rather than sending all 600 does this), and **stream** so the time to the first token is short. Together these changes go after the whole 15-second budget.

whyWrong.A: Batch processing is asynchronous and can take far longer than a live call, so it fails the latency requirement completely.
whyWrong.B: Caching can cut the time spent processing the repeated prefix, but the largest model at maximum effort with no streaming still makes the agent wait for a long full response.
whyWrong.C: A matched article summary does not answer the customer's specific question, so quality drops even though the response is fast.

questions.mindset: Tackle latency at every source (model, input, output, streaming) and verify quality with an eval rather than assuming it.

questions.stem: A 600-person consulting firm wants its consultants to use Claude for drafting, summarizing and research across documents the firm already keeps in common workplace tools. IT has two developers, needs single sign-on and central admin controls, and wants a rollout within a month. Which TWO decisions are the BEST fit? Choose TWO.

options.text: Adopt a managed Claude plan for organizations, such as Team or Enterprise, and use its built-in admin controls and connectors rather than building a custom chat application
Build a custom chat front end on the API with an in-house retrieval pipeline over all firm documents, so that every part of the experience is under the firm's own control
Train a custom model on the firm's past deliverables before launch so the assistant already knows the firm's methods and writing style on the first day of use
Keep custom API development for specific workflows the managed product cannot cover, and decide which ones to build only after usage data shows where the gaps are
Design a multi-agent system with a dedicated specialist agent for each of the firm's practice areas, coordinated by a central orchestrator agent on top of them

questions.explanation: This is a **build-versus-buy** decision. The need is general knowledge work, the timeline is short, the team is small, and SSO and admin controls are required. A managed Claude plan meets all of that without engineering effort. Custom API work should be saved for specific high-value workflows that real usage shows the product cannot handle.

whyWrong.B: Two developers cannot build, secure and run a custom chat app with retrieval and SSO within a month, and it would duplicate what a managed product already offers.
whyWrong.C: Training a custom model is slow and expensive, and the general drafting and research needs here do not call for it.
whyWrong.E: This is over-engineered architecture for a general productivity need, and the team is too small to build or maintain it.

questions.mindset: Buy for general productivity, build for differentiated workflows, and let usage data decide what to build.

questions.stem: A property firm wants to pull about 25 key terms (rent schedule, renewal options, break clauses) out of 5,000 commercial leases. The leases are PDFs, some with scanned pages and rent tables. Engineering proposes spending four months building a custom OCR and layout-parsing pipeline before trying any LLM work. The sponsor wants to **validate value quickly with minimal upfront engineering**. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Approve the four-month OCR and layout pipeline first, because good extraction depends on clean, normalized text and nothing useful can be tested until that pipeline is finished
Have paralegals retype a sample of leases into plain text, then test Claude only on those clean transcripts so that layout problems do not affect the results
Prototype by sending the PDFs straight to Claude, which reads page text and visuals, return a fixed field schema, score it on 100 labeled leases, then decide on preprocessing
Give an agent access to the lease folder and let it decide which terms matter for each lease, without a fixed schema, so that it can adapt to the variety of lease formats

questions.explanation: Claude's PDF support handles text along with visual content such as tables and charts. The quickest way to find out whether the project is worth doing is to **prototype on real documents and measure**: a fixed output schema, a labeled sample, and field-level accuracy. If particular page types fail, the team can then target preprocessing at that measured gap rather than building a large pipeline on a guess.

whyWrong.A: It spends four months before learning whether the approach delivers value, and it may build preprocessing the model does not need.
whyWrong.B: Testing on retyped transcripts hides the real input conditions (scans and tables), so the results would not predict production performance.
whyWrong.D: Without a fixed schema, the outputs can't be scored, compared or loaded into downstream systems, and the business still needs the same 25 terms from every lease.

questions.mindset: Prototype on real inputs, measure against a labeled sample, and add engineering only where the data shows a gap.

questions.stem: A support pipeline runs a Claude agent on each inbound email. The agent creates a ticket in the tracker and sends the customer an acknowledgment through tools. When a run times out, the orchestrator retries the whole run from the beginning, and customers now sometimes get two acknowledgments while duplicate tickets pile up. Which change MOST reliably fixes this?

options.text: Add an instruction to the system prompt telling the agent to check first whether it has already created a ticket or sent an acknowledgment before taking either action
Make the side-effecting tools idempotent with a key based on the source email ID, and record finished steps so a retry continues the run instead of repeating it
Turn off automatic retries entirely, so a run that times out is simply dropped and never processed again, and nothing can ever be duplicated by a retry
Raise the run timeout considerably and switch to a larger, more capable model so that runs finish sooner and fewer of them ever reach the retry step

questions.explanation: Retries are normal in production; the official SDKs even retry transient errors automatically. Actions with side effects must therefore be **safe to repeat**. An idempotency key based on the source email ID lets the ticket and email tools spot a repeat and return the earlier result, and checkpointing finished steps lets a retry pick up where the run stopped. This is a deterministic fix in the tool layer and does not depend on the model remembering anything.

whyWrong.A: A fresh retry may not have the earlier run in its context, and a prompt instruction is not a guarantee. Duplicate prevention belongs in code.
whyWrong.C: Dropping timed-out runs means emails go silently unanswered, which trades duplicates for lost customers.
whyWrong.D: Fewer timeouts make duplicates less frequent but do not remove them, and a larger model usually makes runs slower, not faster.

questions.mindset: Assume retries will happen and make every side effect safe to repeat in code.

questions.stem: A finance team's document pipeline sends each invoice to Claude with the same long system prompt (instructions, schema and examples). At month-end it suddenly fires about 20 times its normal request volume. Many calls return 429 errors, and the failed documents are silently dropped. Which TWO changes BEST make the pipeline dependable? Choose TWO.

options.text: Retry any failed call immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds, so that no document is ever dropped no matter how long the month-end overload lasts
Spread the month-end requests across several API keys created in the same organization so that each key gets its own separate share of the rate limit
Send requests through a queue with bounded concurrency, retry 429s after the retry-after wait, and send documents that still fail to a dead-letter queue with an alert
Shorten the system prompt by removing the schema and examples so that each request uses fewer input tokens and fits more comfortably under the limit
Cache the long shared prompt prefix, because for most models cached input tokens do not count toward input-tokens-per-minute limits, which raises effective throughput

questions.explanation: Two things are needed: **smooth and recover**, and **use less of the limit**. A queue with bounded concurrency, retries that honor `retry-after`, and a dead-letter path mean no document is lost silently. Prompt caching of the repeated prefix helps because, for most models, cached reads do not count toward the ITPM rate limit, so the same limit supports more throughput. The docs also suggest ramping traffic gradually to avoid acceleration limits.

whyWrong.A: Immediate tight-loop retries add load during the overload and ignore the wait time the API tells you to use.
whyWrong.B: Rate limits apply at the organization level, so extra keys in the same organization do not add capacity.
whyWrong.D: Removing the schema and examples hurts extraction quality to save tokens when caching offers the same relief without that cost.

questions.mindset: Design for limits: queue, back off as the API tells you, never drop work silently, and cache what repeats.

questions.stem: A product-support assistant scored 94% on its launch eval. Four months later the company launched a new product line, and customer complaints about wrong answers have risen. No alarm fired, because production monitoring tracks only latency and error rates. Which TWO additions to the architecture BEST close this gap? Choose TWO.

options.text: Re-run the original launch eval set every week on a schedule and raise an alert if the overall score falls below the 94% that the assistant achieved at launch
Continuously sample production conversations and score them with automated graders checked against human labels, alerting when quality drops for any product segment
Have the assistant add a confidence score to every answer and alert the team whenever the average reported confidence for the day falls below a set level
Switch to a larger, more capable model automatically whenever the weekly complaint count rises above an agreed threshold set by the support leadership team
Send low-scoring and complained-about conversations to human review, and add the confirmed failures to the regression eval run before each prompt or model change

questions.explanation: This is **drift**: production inputs changed and the offline eval no longer represents them. The feedback loop needs to watch quality on live traffic, not just system health. Sampled production conversations scored by calibrated graders, split by segment, catch drops early. Human-confirmed failures then go into the regression suite, so the eval grows to cover the new product line and future changes are tested against it.

whyWrong.A: The launch set contains no questions about the new product line, so it can keep scoring 94% while users get wrong answers.
whyWrong.C: A model's self-reported confidence is not a reliable measure of correctness, and it can stay high while the answers are wrong.
whyWrong.D: Switching models in reaction to complaints is untested and expensive, and it does not show what is failing or why.

questions.mindset: Watch quality on live traffic, not just uptime, and turn confirmed production failures into regression tests.

questions.stem: An invoice-coding pipeline auto-approves Claude's general-ledger code whenever Claude reports its own confidence as 0.9 or higher, and reviewers see only the lower-confidence items. A quarterly audit finds a cluster of miscoded invoices, all of which had been auto-approved with high reported confidence. Which redesign of the review stage is MOST effective?

options.text: Raise the auto-approval threshold from 0.9 to 0.97 so that only the answers Claude reports being most certain about skip the human review queue from now on
Ask Claude to reason step by step about how sure it is before giving a confidence number, so that its self-reported score becomes better calibrated over time
Route items using deterministic signals such as validation checks, vendor-history mismatches and amount limits, and also review a random sample of auto-approved items
Send every invoice to human review permanently, so that nothing at all can be auto-approved by the pipeline without a reviewer looking at it and signing off first

questions.explanation: The flaw is relying on the model's **self-reported confidence** as the gate, and the audit shows high confidence does not mean correct. Routing should use signals that can be checked: code-level validations, mismatches against a vendor's usual codes, and amount thresholds. A **random audit sample** of auto-approved items measures the escaped-error rate directly, and those findings feed the eval set and the routing rules.

whyWrong.A: A stricter threshold on a poorly calibrated signal still lets confident mistakes through and sends more good items to review.
whyWrong.B: Asking for more reasoning does not turn self-reported confidence into a measured error rate, and the gate is still unverified.
whyWrong.D: Reviewing everything removes the efficiency the pipeline was built for and does not use the deterministic signals available.

questions.mindset: Gate on signals you can verify, and measure what slips through by auditing a random sample of auto-approved work.

questions.stem: A compliance team needs Claude to review a regulatory submission package made of several filings that together are far larger than a single context window. Every finding must point to the page it came from, and nothing may be missed silently. Which processing design is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Split the package into sections in code, extract findings with page references from each section in parallel, then merge and deduplicate them in a step that keeps the references
Send only the first portion of the package that fits in the context window, on the reasoning that the most important material usually appears early in each filing, with the key disclosures
Make a single call containing as much of the package as possible, with a strong instruction to be thorough and to cite a page reference for every finding it reports
Give an autonomous agent the full package with no predefined steps and let it choose on its own which parts are worth reading and in what order to read them

questions.explanation: When input exceeds one context window and completeness matters, use **sectioning (parallelization) followed by synthesis**. Code guarantees every section is processed. Each section's extraction keeps its page references, and a final step merges and deduplicates the findings while preserving those references. The coverage guarantee comes from the pipeline, not from the model's diligence.

whyWrong.B: Cutting off the rest of the package means everything after the first portion is silently skipped, which is exactly the failure the team must avoid.
whyWrong.C: An instruction to be thorough cannot make content outside the context window visible to the model.
whyWrong.D: An agent free to skip parts gives no coverage guarantee and makes it hard to prove that nothing was missed.

questions.mindset: When completeness is required, enforce coverage in the pipeline structure rather than relying on instructions to the model.

questions.stem: A retailer’s web chat assistant calls the Messages API for every customer turn. After the chat service was scaled from one server to a pool behind a load balancer, with servers recycled on each deploy, customers report that the assistant “forgets” what they said a few messages earlier in the same session. The team wants the fix that is MOST reliable with the fewest moving parts. Which architecture change should they make?

options.text: Enable prompt caching on the conversation and rely on the cache to hold the earlier turns, so any server can continue the chat by sending only the newest customer message
Add a system-prompt instruction asking Claude to remember everything the customer has said during the session and refer back to it whenever it answers a later question
Configure sticky sessions on the load balancer so every request from a customer reaches the same server, where the conversation history is kept in that server’s memory
Store each session’s conversation history in a shared data store keyed by session ID, and have whichever server handles the turn load it and include it in the messages array

questions.explanation: The Messages API is **stateless**: each request carries the prior conversational turns in the `messages` parameter, and the model generates the next turn from what it is sent. The application therefore owns conversation state. When one process kept the history in memory that happened to work; with a server pool and recycled servers it does not. The dependable design keeps session history in shared storage that any server can read and resend on every turn.

whyWrong.A: Prompt caching speeds up and discounts processing of a repeated prefix, but the full prefix must still be sent on every request. The cache is short-lived and is not addressable storage for the conversation.
whyWrong.B: Claude can only see what is in the request. No instruction can recover turns that were never sent, so the assistant still forgets.
whyWrong.C: Sticky sessions patch the symptom while a server is alive, but the history still vanishes when that server is recycled on deploy or fails, and the fix depends on load-balancer behavior.

questions.mindset: The API is stateless; your application owns conversation state, and in a multi-server system that state belongs in shared storage, not in a process or a prompt.

questions.stem: An HR policy-research agent takes two to six minutes per request because it makes several tool calls. The web front end keeps the HTTP request open until the agent finishes, the API gateway cuts connections at 60 seconds, and frustrated employees resubmit, which starts duplicate runs. Which architecture change BEST fits?

options.text: Raise the API gateway timeout to ten minutes so the front end can keep the single connection open until even the slowest agent run has finished
Accept the request and return a job ID at once, run the agent in a background worker, show progress or notify on completion, and ignore duplicate submissions
Cap the agent at two tool calls per request so that every run is guaranteed to finish comfortably inside the existing 60-second gateway limit without changes elsewhere
Submit each research request through the Message Batches API and email the employee a link to the answer once the batch has finished processing

questions.explanation: Long-running agent work should be **asynchronous**: accept the job, return a job ID, process it in a worker, and push progress or a completion notice to the user. Deduplicating on the job ID stops resubmissions from starting extra runs. Users get feedback right away, and no request depends on a long-held connection.

whyWrong.A: Long-held connections are fragile because networks may drop idle connections, and users still wait with no feedback, so they still resubmit.
whyWrong.C: Cutting the agent's tool calls to fit the timeout sacrifices answer quality because of a transport problem.
whyWrong.D: Batch results can take much longer to arrive than an interactive user expects, and it removes the in-app experience users are used to.

questions.mindset: Separate long agent work from the user's request through a job queue, and give users progress feedback.

questions.stem: A team edits its production extraction prompt directly in a configuration screen. Last month, an edit that improved tone also broke the JSON output for about 10% of requests, and nobody noticed for three days. The team wants to prevent this kind of regression **with the least ongoing manual effort**. What should they do?

options.text: Require two engineers to read and sign off on every prompt edit before it is saved, so that a second pair of eyes catches any risky wording changes before they reach production
Freeze the production prompt completely and allow no further edits to it at all unless a full quarterly change review has formally approved the change
Version prompts in source control, require a regression eval with schema-validity checks to pass before deployment, then roll out gradually while monitoring
Ask Claude to review each new prompt edit and predict whether the change could break the output format before the edit is allowed to go into production

questions.explanation: Prompts are production code. Putting them under **version control**, gating each change on an **automated regression eval** (with format checks that would have caught the JSON break), and rolling out gradually with monitoring catches regressions before users do. The checks run automatically, which meets the least-manual-effort requirement.

whyWrong.A: Reading a prompt does not show how it behaves on real inputs. The tone edit looked harmless, which is why it slipped through.
whyWrong.B: A freeze blocks improvements and still does not test the changes that are eventually approved.
whyWrong.D: A model's prediction about a prompt is not evidence. Only running the prompt on representative cases shows whether the format breaks.

questions.mindset: Treat prompts as code: version them, test them automatically, and roll them out gradually.

questions.stem: An internal policy Q&A assistant uses retrieval over the HR and finance policy library. Thumbs-down votes and comments collect in a single spreadsheet, and each week the team responds by rewording the system prompt, with no measurable improvement. A review of 50 complaints finds that about half the answers cited outdated policy documents, many came from the retriever missing the right document, and only a few were generation mistakes. Which TWO changes to the feedback loop are MOST effective? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep rewording the system prompt each week, and add a firm instruction to always rely on the most recent version of any policy the assistant happens to retrieve
Use retrieval traces to classify each failure by stage (source content, retrieval or generation) and route it to that stage’s owner, for example stale documents to policy owners
Upgrade to a larger and more capable model so that the assistant can recognize outdated policies and work around retrieval gaps without any other changes
Turn confirmed failures into stage-specific evals, such as whether the right document appears in the top results and whether the answer is grounded, so each fix is measured
Increase the number of retrieved passages from 5 to 50 for every question so that the correct policy document is almost certain to be somewhere in the context the model sees

questions.explanation: The loop is failing because every complaint is treated as a **prompt problem**. A good feedback loop finds which stage failed and sends the fix there. Stale source documents go to the people who own the content, retrieval misses go to retrieval tuning, and only true generation errors go to the prompt. Stage-specific evals (retrieval recall and answer grounding) then show whether each fix actually helped.

whyWrong.A: The prompt cannot fix outdated documents or documents that were never retrieved. That is why weekly rewording has not moved the numbers.
whyWrong.C: A bigger model cannot tell which policy version is current if the outdated document is all it sees, and it cannot use a document that was never retrieved.
whyWrong.E: Fifty passages add cost and noise, can make the model rely on the wrong document, and leave the stale content in the library.

questions.mindset: Diagnose which stage failed and fix it there. Not every quality problem is a prompt problem.
